lessons.title: What Linux Is & Why DevOps Uses It

slots.practicalActivity: On any Linux machine you can reach (even a free online terminal if you haven't set up a lab yet), run uname -a and cat /etc/os-release and write down the exact kernel version, architecture, and distribution reported. Then, for a fictional company standing up its first 10 Linux servers, write a one-paragraph recommendation choosing a distribution family (Debian/Ubuntu vs. RHEL/Rocky) citing the same 3 criteria the lesson used — cost, team familiarity, and cloud image support.
slots.deliverable: Real uname -a and /etc/os-release output from a Linux machine, plus a written distribution recommendation for a 10-server fleet citing cost, familiarity, and cloud support.

slots.practicalActivity: Set up a real, persistent Linux lab you'll use for the rest of this course: install WSL2 with Ubuntu (Windows) or create an Ubuntu Server VM in VirtualBox (any OS). Once it's running, run whoami, hostname, and uname -a to confirm you've actually landed in a real Linux shell, not just a lookalike prompt.
slots.deliverable: A working Linux lab environment (WSL2 or a VirtualBox VM) with whoami, hostname, and uname -a output confirming it's a genuine Linux shell you'll keep using going forward.

slots.practicalActivity: On your lab machine, run ls -la / and df -h to see the real top-level directory tree and what's mounted where. Then explore 5 of the directories from the lesson's table yourself (ls /etc, ls /var/log, ls /home, ls /opt, ls /tmp) and write one real sentence for each about what you actually found there, confirming or correcting what the lesson said should live in it.
slots.deliverable: Real ls -la / and df -h output from your lab machine, plus 5 written sentences describing what you actually found inside /etc, /var/log, /home, /opt, and /tmp.

slots.practicalActivity: On your lab machine, practice pwd, cd with both absolute and relative paths, cd ~, cd -, and cd .. until each feels automatic — navigate to /etc, then /var/log, then back home with ~, then back to /var/log with cd -. Run ls -la on your home directory and ls -lh /var/log to practice reading the long-format, hidden-file, and human-readable flags, and use Tab completion at least 5 times on real paths.
slots.deliverable: A terminal history (copy-pasted or screenshotted) showing at least 8 real navigation commands including cd with an absolute path, cd with a relative path, cd -, and ls -la / ls -lh against real directories.

slots.practicalActivity: On your lab machine, build the same kind of structure the lesson did: mkdir -p app/logs/2026 in one command, touch a CHANGELOG.md, cp it into app/, use cp -r to back up the whole app directory, then mv/rename files, and finally create 4 fake log files named with a date pattern (deploy-2026-10-0{1,2,3,4}.log) and use a single wildcard mv command to move all of them into a new app/logs/archive directory.
slots.deliverable: A real app/ directory tree on your lab machine containing a changelog, a backup copy made with cp -r, and an archive subdirectory populated using one wildcard mv command moving 4 files at once.

slots.practicalActivity: Using the log files you created last session, practice cat on the short changelog, less on a longer file (page through with Space/b, search with /, quit with q), and head/tail with -n on the archived logs. Start a background process that appends a line to a log file every few seconds (or use `yes "test line" | head -20 >> test.log` repeated) and use tail -f to watch it grow live, then stop it with Ctrl+C. Finally, run grep -in against your logs for a keyword and wc -l to count a file's lines.
slots.deliverable: Terminal output showing cat, less (with at least one search), head and tail -n, a tail -f session that was actually followed and stopped, plus a grep -in search and a wc -l count, all against real files you created.

slots.practicalActivity: On your lab machine, create a hard link to one of your files and a symbolic link to your app/logs/archive directory, confirming with ls -li that the hard link shares an inode number with its original. Then package your whole app/ directory with tar -czf into a single compressed archive, extract it into a new location to confirm it round-trips correctly, and repeat the same packaging with zip/unzip for comparison.
slots.deliverable: ls -li output proving a hard link shares an inode with its source, a working symlink, and a tar.gz archive plus a zip archive of the same directory, both successfully extracted back into their original files.

slots.practicalActivity: Create a fake nginx.conf-style text file and edit it in nano: add 2 lines, use Ctrl+K to cut one line and Ctrl+U to paste it back, then save with Ctrl+O and exit with Ctrl+X. Open the same file in vim, press i to enter insert mode, make an edit, press Esc to return to normal mode, use dd to delete a line and yy/p to copy and paste another, then save and quit with :wq. Reopen it, make a throwaway change, and practice discarding it with :q!.
slots.deliverable: A text file that was edited and saved in nano using Ctrl+K/Ctrl+U/Ctrl+O/Ctrl+X, then further edited and saved in vim using insert mode, dd, yy/p, and :wq, plus confirmation that :q! correctly discarded an unwanted change.

slots.practicalActivity: On your lab machine, run ls -l against 3 of your own files and read out the full 10-character permission string for each. Use chmod in symbolic mode (u+x, g-w) on one file and in octal mode (750, 644) on two others, confirming the change with ls -l each time. Check your current umask with umask, then touch a new file and mkdir a new directory, confirming their default permissions match the 666/777-minus-umask math.
slots.deliverable: ls -l output for 3 files before and after chmod changes made in both symbolic and octal notation, plus your real umask value and the default permissions it produced on a freshly created file and directory.

slots.practicalActivity: On your lab VM, grep your own username out of /etc/passwd and (with sudo) /etc/shadow, identifying each colon-separated field. Create a new group with groupadd, create a new user with useradd -m -s /bin/bash -G, set its password with passwd, then use usermod -aG to add it to a second group, and confirm its full identity and group membership with both id and groups.
slots.deliverable: Your own /etc/passwd and /etc/shadow entries with fields labeled, plus a newly created user and group on your lab VM, confirmed with id and groups showing correct primary and supplementary group membership.

slots.practicalActivity: On your lab VM, run sudo -l to see your own current sudo access. Using sudo visudo (never a plain text editor), add a scoped rule for the test user you created last session granting it NOPASSWD access to exactly one command (e.g. /usr/bin/systemctl status nginx), then switch to that user and confirm the scoped command runs without a password prompt while an unlisted command still asks for one.
slots.deliverable: sudo -l output before and after editing /etc/sudoers with visudo, plus proof that your test user can run the one NOPASSWD-scoped command without a prompt while any other sudo command still prompts for a password.

slots.practicalActivity: Create a shared directory on your lab VM, chmod g+s it to set setgid, and confirm (as a different user, or by checking the group on a new file you create inside it) that new files inherit the directory's group instead of the creator's primary group. Then chmod +t a second scratch directory to set the sticky bit and explain in one sentence what it would prevent. Finally, use setfacl to grant one extra user read+execute access to a file without changing its owner or group, and confirm the grant with getfacl.
slots.deliverable: A directory with setgid confirmed by a new file inheriting its group, a second directory with the sticky bit set, and an ACL grant on a file confirmed with getfacl showing the extra user's permission entry.

slots.practicalActivity: Chapter-ending permissions lab for Permissions, Users & Groups: create 2 new users and a shared group on your lab VM, build one shared project directory owned by that group with setgid set so new files always inherit it, grant sudo access to one of the two users for exactly one command via visudo, and grant a third, separate user read-only ACL access to the shared directory without making them a group member — verifying every piece with ls -l, id, sudo -l, and getfacl.
slots.deliverable: A fully configured shared multi-user permissions setup — 2 users, a group, a setgid shared directory, one scoped sudo rule, and one ACL grant — each piece verified with the matching inspection command.

slots.practicalActivity: On your lab VM, pipe ps aux into grep to find a real running process, then redirect a command's output to a file with >, append a second line with >>, and deliberately trigger an error to practice capturing it with 2> and merging it with 2>&1 so both streams land in one file.
slots.deliverable: Terminal output showing a working pipe, a > overwrite, a >> append, a captured 2> error, and a combined 2>&1 redirect, each demonstrated with a real command on your lab VM.

slots.practicalActivity: Create a sample log file with at least 20 lines mixing INFO, WARN, and ERROR entries. Use grep with -i, -v, -n, and -c to isolate and count different categories, use sed 's/old/new/' to preview a text substitution and then sed -i to apply it for real, and use awk to extract one specific field from each line and pipe it into sort | uniq -c to rank how often each value appears.
slots.deliverable: A real sample log file processed with all 4 grep flags (-i, -v, -n, -c), a sed substitution applied with -i, and an awk one-liner whose output was ranked with sort | uniq -c.

slots.practicalActivity: In a disposable scratch directory on your lab VM, create a mix of files with different extensions, sizes, and ages (fake age with touch -d). Use find with -name, -type, -size, and -mtime to filter matches, pipe results into xargs ls -la to preview them, then use -exec and a find-to-xargs rm -v pipeline to actually delete the stale ones. Then create a small personal script in ~/bin, export PATH="$HOME/bin:$PATH", and confirm with which that your script now runs by name from any directory; make the PATH change permanent by adding it to ~/.bashrc and reloading with source.
slots.deliverable: A scratch directory of mixed test files with find output showing -name/-type/-size/-mtime filters, proof that -exec and a find-to-xargs pipeline both acted on the matches, plus a script in a custom directory that runs by bare name after being added to PATH permanently via ~/.bashrc.

slots.practicalActivity: On your lab VM, run ps aux | grep for a real running process and note its PID, %CPU, and STAT columns, then watch the same data live in top. Start a long-running command (e.g. sleep 300) in the background with &, list it with jobs, bring it to the foreground with fg, then background a second one with nohup so it would survive a logout. Finally, start a third dummy process, send it SIGTERM with kill, and practice finding and signaling a process by name with pgrep and pkill instead of its PID.
slots.deliverable: Real ps aux and top output identifying a specific process's PID and resource usage, plus proof of backgrounding a job with &, using jobs/fg, detaching one with nohup, and stopping a process by name with pkill.

slots.practicalActivity: Write a minimal custom systemd unit file for a trivial script of your own (even a one-liner that sleeps and loops, writing a timestamp to a file every few seconds), place it in /etc/systemd/system/, run sudo systemctl daemon-reload, then sudo systemctl enable --now it. Confirm it's running with systemctl status, then practice stop, start, and restart, and confirm enable actually persists across a reboot by checking systemctl is-enabled.
slots.deliverable: A real custom .service unit file for your own script, successfully enabled and started with systemctl enable --now, with systemctl status confirming it's active and systemctl is-enabled confirming it will survive a reboot.

slots.practicalActivity: Add a real crontab entry with crontab -e that appends a timestamp to a log file every minute (*/1 * * * *), confirm it's running by checking the log file growing over a few minutes, then remove it. Next, build the systemd-timer equivalent: a paired .service and .timer unit that runs the same task on a schedule, enable the timer with systemctl enable --now, and confirm it with systemctl list-timers.
slots.deliverable: A working cron job proven to run on schedule (log file growing over several minutes) and its systemd-timer equivalent (paired .service/.timer units) confirmed scheduled with systemctl list-timers.

slots.practicalActivity: Run journalctl -u against the custom service you built 2 sessions ago, then filter it with --since, -p err, and -f (following it live while you restart the service in a second terminal). Then run top, free -h, df -h, du -sh on a directory with several files, and uptime on your lab VM, writing down the current load average and explaining in one sentence whether your VM is under pressure given its CPU core count.
slots.deliverable: journalctl output filtered by unit, time range, and severity for your own service, a live -f session captured around a restart, plus top/free/df/du/uptime output from your lab VM with a one-sentence load-average assessment.

slots.practicalActivity: On your lab VM, run apt update (or dnf makecache), then apt search for a real package you don't have installed (e.g. htop), install it with apt install, confirm it with apt list --installed | grep, and finally remove it with apt remove. If your distro is RHEL-family instead, run the equivalent dnf search/install/remove sequence and write one sentence comparing the exact command differences you hit.
slots.deliverable: A real package searched for, installed, confirmed as installed, and removed using apt or dnf on your lab VM, with the exact commands and their output captured.

slots.practicalActivity: On your lab VM, run lsblk to see your disk and partition layout, then df -h to see what's mounted where. In VirtualBox, attach a second virtual disk to your VM, then inside the VM use blkid to find its UUID once it has a filesystem, mkdir a mount point, mount it manually, add a matching UUID-based entry to /etc/fstab, and run sudo mount -a to validate the entry works before ever rebooting.
slots.deliverable: lsblk and df -h output from your lab VM, plus proof of a second disk being partitioned, mounted manually, added to /etc/fstab by UUID, and validated with mount -a without errors.

slots.practicalActivity: Generate a real SSH key pair with ssh-keygen -t ed25519, and connect it to your own lab VM (via ssh-copy-id if you're connecting from a separate host, or by manually appending your public key to ~/.ssh/authorized_keys if the VM is local). Confirm you can log in with no password prompt, then copy a file to and from the VM with scp, and set up a ~/.ssh/config entry so you can connect by a short host alias instead of typing the full address.
slots.deliverable: A real SSH key pair generated and installed on your lab VM proven by a no-password login, a file copied in each direction with scp, and a working ~/.ssh/config shortcut that connects with a short alias.

slots.practicalActivity: On your lab VM, with your SSH key login from last session already confirmed working, edit /etc/ssh/sshd_config to set PasswordAuthentication no and PermitRootLogin no, validate the file with sudo sshd -t, and reload (not restart) the service — keeping your original session open while you test a fresh connection in a second terminal. Then enable ufw (or firewalld), allowing SSH explicitly before turning the firewall on, and confirm its status shows active with a default-deny policy.
slots.deliverable: An sshd_config with password authentication and root login disabled, validated and reloaded without losing access, plus an enabled firewall (ufw or firewalld) showing an explicit SSH allow rule under a default-deny policy.

slots.practicalActivity: Write a real check-disk.sh script with a #!/bin/bash shebang, a header comment block, and logic that reports the root filesystem's usage percentage and prints a WARNING if it's above an 80% threshold (using df -h / and awk to extract the usage number, as in the lesson). Run it two ways: once with bash check-disk.sh, and once after chmod +x with ./check-disk.sh, then check $? after each run.
slots.deliverable: A real, executable check-disk.sh script with a shebang, header comment, and an 80% usage threshold warning, run successfully both via bash and via ./ after chmod +x, with $? checked after each.

slots.practicalActivity: Extend last session's script (or write a new backup.sh) using variables for a server name and a backup directory path, and an if/elif/else block that creates the backup directory with mkdir -p if it doesn't exist, confirms it's writable if it does, or exits 1 with an error message if it isn't. Add one short-circuit guard line using || (e.g. cd "$backup_dir" || exit 1) and test the script in both the "directory doesn't exist yet" and "directory already exists" states.
slots.deliverable: A real backup.sh script using variables and if/elif/else to handle a directory that doesn't exist, exists and is writable, and exists but isn't writable, plus one working || guard line, tested in at least two of those states.

slots.practicalActivity: Write a script with a for loop that iterates over a list of 3 fake server names and echoes a status line for each, and a separate while loop that counts from 0 to 4. Then write a restart_service function (modeled on the lesson's example) that takes a service name as $1, uses local for its internal variable, attempts systemctl restart on it, and returns 0 or 1 based on whether systemctl is-active confirms it came back up — call the function from an if statement that prints a different message for success vs. failure.
slots.deliverable: A script containing a working for loop over a list, a working while loop with a counter, and a restart_service function using local and a tested return value, called correctly from an if statement.

slots.practicalActivity: Write a deploy.sh that prints $0, $1, $2, $@, and $#, and exits with a usage message if $# is less than 1. Write a second script, restart-all.sh, that accepts an unknown number of server names and uses a while [ "$#" -gt 0 ] loop with shift to process them one at a time. Add a read -p prompt to ask for a server name interactively, and a basic getopts loop parsing a -e <env> flag plus a -v on/off flag, testing it with a real command line like ./deploy.sh -e staging -v.
slots.deliverable: A deploy.sh demonstrating $0/$1/$@/$#, a restart-all.sh using shift to process an unknown number of arguments, a read -p interactive prompt, and a working getopts loop tested with a real -e/-v command line.

slots.practicalActivity: Take one of your earlier scripts and add set -euo pipefail as its second line, then deliberately introduce a failing command and a reference to an unset/misspelled variable to confirm the script now stops immediately on each, rather than continuing silently. Add a trap 'rm -f "$tmpfile"' EXIT line around a real mktemp-created temp file so it's cleaned up no matter how the script exits, and run the whole script with bash -x to trace every command.
slots.deliverable: A script with set -euo pipefail proven to stop on both a failing command and an unset variable, a working trap EXIT cleanup for a real temp file, and a captured bash -x trace of the full script running.

lessons.title: Capstone Kickoff: Set Up and Harden a Linux Server

slots.practicalActivity: Write out the full capstone plan for your own lab server before touching it: the exact order of the 7 steps (users & groups, SSH key access, firewall, root login disabled, a systemd service, a cron job, log review), and for each of the 3 ordering traps the lesson calls out (test SSH keys before disabling passwords; confirm sudo before locking out root; allow SSH before enabling the firewall), write one sentence explaining what breaks if you did it in the wrong order.
slots.deliverable: A written, ordered 7-step capstone plan for your lab server, plus 3 written sentences explaining the specific lockout risk of doing each of the 3 ordering-sensitive steps out of sequence.

slots.practicalActivity: On your lab VM, execute the full build from your kickoff plan in the correct order: create a sudo-capable user and confirm sudo whoami returns root; generate and install an SSH key and confirm passwordless login in a fresh terminal before touching anything else; disable PermitRootLogin and PasswordAuthentication, validating with sshd -t and reloading; enable ufw with SSH allowed first; wrap a small script of your own in a systemd service with Restart=on-failure; and schedule a nightly cron job redirecting both stdout and stderr to a log file.
slots.deliverable: A fully built and hardened lab server: a working sudo user, SSH key-only login with root login and password auth disabled, an enabled default-deny firewall, a running systemd-managed service, and a scheduled cron job logging its output.

slots.practicalActivity: Run the lesson's full 8-item verification checklist against your own build (groups, SSH login, sshd -T for both root login and password auth, ufw status verbose, systemctl is-enabled/is-active for your service, your crontab -l, and a journalctl check for accepted key-based logins with no accepted root logins), fixing anything that doesn't match. Then write your own resume bullet naming the specific tools you used, and a short README for the project listing what it does and which files are included.
slots.deliverable: Output from all 8 verification checklist items run against your own hardened server, confirming every requirement actually took effect, plus a written resume bullet and a project README naming the specific tools used.

monthlyMilestoneContribution: A student finishing this course can work entirely from the Linux command line on a real server — navigating the filesystem, managing permissions/users/groups, chaining pipes and text tools, controlling processes and systemd services, scheduling jobs, connecting over SSH with keys, and writing a real Bash script with arguments, error handling, and cleanup — and has personally hardened and verified one server end to end.
